name: David Cameron
role: UK Prime Minister (2010-2016), Conservative leader (2005-2016); Foreign Secretary (2023-2024)
summary: Cameron led a modernising, pro-market Conservative Party and governed first in coalition and then alone, pairing deficit reduction, welfare conditionality and tighter immigration control with support for the NHS, overseas aid and same-sex marriage. He favoured a looser, reformed EU membership, a strong NATO and Trident, humanitarian military intervention, and localist public-service reform through the Big Society.

universal-healthcare.rationale: The 2015 manifesto he led pledges a truly 7-day NHS free to patients and rising NHS spending; his governments ring-fenced NHS budgets and he cites the NHS funding increase in the Commons.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: As Prime Minister he introduced the national living wage on top of the minimum wage, citing the 50p rise and tougher enforcement, though he frames growth as the main route to higher pay.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: His 2010 economy speech promised to free enterprise rather than control business, and at Davos in 2013 he backed open economies, low taxes and free enterprise within enforced rules.

public-ownership.rationale: He privatised Royal Mail and defended the sale in the Commons, and the 2015 manifesto continues selling government stakes in bailed-out banks.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: His government cut the top income tax rate from 50p to 45p, which he defended as raising more revenue, and the 2015 manifesto raised the inheritance tax threshold and the 40p threshold.

regulate-corporations.rationale: He pledged one-in, two-out on new regulations and cutting red tape, but also said free enterprise needs enforced rules and backed tax transparency, so the evidence points both ways.

cut-welfare.rationale: He introduced the benefit cap and argued that the welfare system trapped people in dependency, while protecting pensioner benefits and the NHS, so he backed cutting working-age welfare in particular.

surveillance-ok.rationale: He passed emergency data retention legislation in 2014 and said terrorists must not have a safe space to communicate; the manifesto keeps the ability to intercept suspects' communications.

state-harmful.rationale: The manifesto he led describes the intended state as neither smaller than needed nor bigger than affordable and commits to NHS, schools and pensions, a position at odds with the state being unnecessary.

empower-police-military.rationale: He pledged 2% of GDP on defence, new surveillance drones and counter-terror powers, but said police reform was set back by the idea that officer numbers mattered more than smart deployment, so the evidence is mixed.

decide-locally.rationale: His Big Society speech called for pushing power away from central to local government and new community powers to run local services, and he cites the Localism Act.

rehabilitation.rationale: In his prison speech he called punishment not a dirty word while also making reform a progressive cause, and in 2011 he promised prisons of punishment with a purpose.

traditional-family.rationale: The manifesto backs the institution of marriage through a transferable allowance and names family breakdown as a root cause of poverty, but he also championed same-sex marriage.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: He drove the Marriage (Same Sex Couples) Act 2013 and said in the Commons he was proud of it and that marriage is for a man and a woman, two men or two women.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: The manifesto heading says the party will protect British values and our way of life, and at Munich he said Britain had weakened its collective identity.

reduce-immigration.rationale: He pledged to bring net migration down from hundreds of thousands to tens of thousands and introduced a cap on economic migrants from outside the EU.

free-trade.rationale: At Bloomberg he called for transformative trade deals with the US, Japan and India toward global free trade, and at the G20 he said he was fighting protectionism.

nation-first.rationale: In 2024 he said the national interest defines foreign policy but argued that Britain's interest is best served through alliances and cooperation, so evidence points both ways.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: He led the 2011 Libya intervention and defended it in the Commons as a humanitarian intervention to stop the slaughter of innocent people.

open-borders.rationale: He criticised an open-door immigration system and said a strong country controls immigration rather than pulling up the drawbridge.

limit-growth.rationale: He treated a strong economy as the means of paying for environmental measures and rejected curbs such as refusing new North Sea licences in 2024.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: He urged a legally binding global climate agreement at COP21 and cited carbon budgets, but also stopped onshore wind subsidies and called for a proportionate approach in 2024.

expand-nuclear.rationale: The manifesto promises a significant expansion in new nuclear, backing Hinkley Point, and he said in the Commons that strong nuclear energy should be at the heart of the system.

tax-inheritance.rationale: The manifesto promised to take the family home out of inheritance tax by raising the effective threshold to 1 million pounds for couples, and he defended passing wealth down generations.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: He told the Commons he was part of the consensus to stop the march to protectionism and in 2023 lamented that protectionism was replacing free trade.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: In his Commons motion for the Queen's 90th birthday he praised her service and said she brought the monarchy closer to the people while retaining its dignity.

democracy-best.rationale: He called for the building blocks of democracy abroad, praised Israel's Knesset as a beacon of democracy, and after losing the 2016 referendum said the result must be respected.

direct-votes.rationale: He argued big constitutional questions such as the EU and Scotland should go to the people, but routine lawmaking stayed with Parliament, so the evidence points both ways.

right-to-secede.rationale: On Scottish independence he said the choice was squarely and solely for Scotland's people to make and agreed a legal referendum, while arguing against leaving.

separate-church-state.rationale: He told the Commons that Britain is a Christian country and that its established faith makes it more tolerant, defending the established church.

military-superiority.rationale: He kept defence at 2% of GDP, announced new strike brigades and drones in 2015 and in 2024 urged staying at the cutting edge of defence technology.

ethnic-nation.rationale: He described Britain as one of the most successful multi-ethnic, multi-faith democracies in the world and rejected the hard right's call for repatriation at Munich.

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: He said terrorists should not have a safe space to communicate and the manifesto keeps the power to intercept suspects' communications.

territorial-expansion.rationale: In 2024 he set out principles of right not might and respect for sovereignty and territorial integrity, condemning Russia's invasion of Ukraine.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: In the Knesset he affirmed the right of the Jewish people to live a peaceful and prosperous life in Israel after their long search for a nation.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: He made cutting the deficit the core of his 2010 programme, told Davos leaders to deal with their debts, and the manifesto commits to a budget surplus.

force-without-un.rationale: He told the Commons that if a Security Council veto blocks action, Britain should reserve the ability to act in its national or humanitarian interest.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: He sought to bar EU migrants from tax credits for four years and to restrict benefits for new arrivals, though not reserving all welfare for citizens.

work-for-welfare.rationale: The manifesto requires young claimants to take an apprenticeship, traineeship or daily community work for their benefits, and his welfare speech asked what contribution should be expected from those receiving benefits.

proportional-representation.rationale: He told the Commons in 2009 that proportional representation is a recipe for weak coalition governments.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He defended the NHS, schools, pensions and a welfare system, calling for a state of the right size, not one limited to defence, justice and property.

population-transfer.rationale: At Munich he rejected forced repatriation of Muslims, favoured by some fascists, as part of an Islamophobic argument.

right-to-buy-council-homes.rationale: The manifesto extends the Right to Buy to housing association tenants, and he cites it among his housing record.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: The manifesto requires strikes to rest on a ballot with at least half of the workforce voting and tougher thresholds in essential services.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: He named debt, family breakdown, educational failure, worklessness and addiction as the roots of poverty, not population growth.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: He said state multiculturalism had weakened identity and that fast change strains communities, yet he praised diversity as a strength and rejected the idea that migrants harm cohesion.

party-controls-media.rationale: The manifesto calls a free media the bedrock of an open society, and he cited a free media as a building block of democracy at Davos.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: He campaigned to stay in the EU but rejected ever closer union and sought a flexible Europe with powers returned, so he accepted existing pooling but opposed more.

recall-officials.rationale: He said voters should be able to recall MPs engaged in wrongdoing, and the government passed the Recall of MPs Act, though only with a cause.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: He hosted the 2014 NATO summit, called alliances central to defence, and in 2024 said Article 5 trust is key to NATO's strength.

death-penalty.rationale: As Prime Minister he told the Commons that opposing the death penalty in all circumstances is long-standing policy, and in 2024 he said the UK opposes it in every circumstance.

restrict-pornography.rationale: His 2013 speech announced adult-content filters on phones by default, threatened legislation on search engines and proposed criminalising possession of simulated rape pornography.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: He met the 0.7 per cent of income aid target, called aid vital to progress against disease and poverty, and listed it with the defence pledge as a promise kept.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: He told the Commons that maintaining Britain's independent nuclear deterrent is right and the manifesto commits to building four successor submarines.

central-bank-independence.rationale: The manifesto credits supervision led by the independent Bank of England, and he said Britain's monetary policy is set independently by the Bank.

collective-defense.rationale: In 2024 he said Article 5 is the key to NATO and that allies must stand up for each other in opposing aggression.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: He told the Commons that the Crimea referendum was illegitimate and illegal and that Russia's action was effectively annexing another country's territory.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: On Magna Carta's 800th anniversary he stressed limits on executive power, rule of law and governments subject to the law.

common-currency.rationale: He said Britain keeps independent monetary policy via the Bank of England and that he opposes joining the euro ever, preferring a single market without a single currency.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: He said poverty cannot be eradicated by aid alone and urged trade, tax transparency and investment in poor countries alongside a 0.7 per cent aid budget, not instead of it.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: At Munich he cited the street demands in Tunis and Cairo as proof of a universal right to free elections and democracy.

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: In 2024 he cited the National Security Investment Act, which screens investment into critical national infrastructure, as part of defending against hostile states.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: He told the Commons that lifting the EU arms embargo on the Syrian opposition was right, to send a signal against Assad.

non-intervention.rationale: He argued that states may act on humanitarian grounds without UN sanction, as in Libya, rejecting any absolute bar on intervention.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: He rejected the far right's clash of civilizations framing at Munich and challenged extremist conspiracy theories against Muslims and Jews.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: He told the Commons he wanted to back marriage in the tax system and the manifesto introduces a transferable allowance for married couples and civil partners.

national-law-over-international.rationale: The manifesto breaks the formal link between British courts and the ECHR and makes the Supreme Court the ultimate arbiter, and in 2024 he said such questions should be decided by accountable politicians.

religious-nation.rationale: He said Britain is a Christian country but also stressed that it is a multi-faith democracy, so he did not define the nation by one religion.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: His Big Society speech opened public services to charities, social enterprises and private companies, and his 2011 NHS speech urged opening the NHS to new ideas.

holocaust-denial.rationale: In the Knesset he said he wanted every British child to learn about the Holocaust and set up a Holocaust Commission.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: He called for proper rights for LGBT people worldwide, criticised states that persecute gay people, apologised for Section 28 and legalised same-sex marriage.

suppress-opposition.rationale: On Egypt in 2011 he rejected a choice between a security state and an Islamist one and backed free elections and democracy.

participatory-democracy.rationale: His Big Society agenda created community rights to take over local services and gave people data to act, aiming at a huge redistribution of power.

assisted-dying.rationale: He told the Commons in 2015 that he did not support the assisted dying proposals or euthanasia, citing pressure on frail elderly people.

islam-incompatible.rationale: At Munich he said Islamist extremism is the problem, not Islam, and that Western values and Islam are compatible.

social-market-economy.rationale: He backed open economies and low taxes with enforced rules of the game, alongside a protected NHS and welfare safety net.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He pledged to keep the armed forces strong, maintain the regular army above 82,000 and sustain 2% defence spending.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: He called NATO membership a cornerstone of defence policy and in 2024 championed its Article 5 guarantee.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: He praised Magna Carta for the rule of law, written limits on rulers and no imprisonment without trial.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: In his prison speech he said serious offenders must go to jail and argued for a more effective prison system rather than abolition.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: He called Northern Ireland's power-sharing one of the most inspiring things he had seen and backed devolving justice powers to Stormont.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: His Big Society policy opened services to charities and social enterprises, and the manifesto praises faith groups and charities as part of society's fabric.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: He said he is a strong supporter of women bishops and urged the Church of England to move forward.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: He said many in Scotland support keeping the nuclear deterrent and its jobs, and the manifesto retains the Trident submarine deterrent.

second-chamber.rationale: The manifesto says the House of Lords should fulfil its valuable role in scrutiny and revision and sees a case for an elected element.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He led the NATO-backed Libya intervention to protect civilians and pushed for airstrikes against ISIL in Syria, not only defence of Britain.

free-public-college.rationale: The manifesto defends his government's university funding reforms, under which students pay nothing while studying and repay only above an income threshold, rather than tuition being free.

future-generations.rationale: At COP21 he warned against making excuses to children and grandchildren and urged action on climate change today.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: He announced a charter of budget responsibility to entrench strong public finances and stop borrowing in a boom.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: He called the deterrent the ultimate insurance policy in a dangerous world and attacked a Labour leader who campaigned for unilateral disarmament.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: In 2011 he proposed mandatory life sentences for the most serious repeat offenders and a mandatory sentence for threatening with a knife.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: The manifesto says speaking English is a fundamental part of integration and cites tough language tests for migrants.

women-suffrage.rationale: In the Commons he recalled what the suffragettes achieved and the achievement of universal suffrage as a cause for pride.

national-church-status.rationale: He said Britain's established faith and the place of faith in national life make it more tolerant, endorsing the established status of the Church of England.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: He backed the Falkland Islanders' referendum as an exercise in self-determination, while calling the Crimea vote under Russian guns illegitimate.

close-ties-china.rationale: He pursued close China ties as Prime Minister, but in 2024 he warned of Chinese spying and an axis of authoritarian states.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: His coalition raised VAT from 17.5 to 20 per cent, and the manifesto promised no further VAT rises rather than cuts.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: He kept universal pensioner benefits, saying he was elected to protect them, while capping working-age benefits, so he neither targeted nor kept all spending universal.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: He told the Commons he supported a financial transaction tax at global level, while criticising European leaders for treating it as an EU revenue source.

notes: Positions are taken from his own speeches, the 2015 manifesto he led and his recorded Commons and Lords statements. His EU stance moved from reform to a referendum he lost, and he accepted the result. His China stance was warmer as Prime Minister than as Foreign Secretary in 2024, where the later view counts. His government's legislation is treated as his only where he personally drove or stated it.
